requirements.requirement: Configure node1 so only root and opsadmin can schedule cron jobs (via cron.allow/cron.deny)
requirements.summary: opsadmin user created; /etc/cron.allow set to root+opsadmin (root:root, 644); /etc/cron.deny removed to avoid ambiguity. Baseline confirmed no prior cron.allow/cron.deny and no opsadmin user existed before the change.

requirements.requirement: Verify enforcement: non-listed users denied crontab access, root/opsadmin allowed
requirements.summary: Using correct user-impersonation (sudo -n -u <user> crontab -l/-), cronprobe2 and precheck were denied with 'not allowed to use this program (crontab)'; opsadmin and root successfully installed/listed crontab entries. Note: an earlier verification for 'cronprobe' used 'crontab -u cronprobe -' run as root, which does not test per-user restriction (root can install for any user regardless of cron.allow) and produced a misleading 'exit 0' result plus a stray spool file for cronprobe; this was corrected by the subsequent cronprobe2 test and the stray file was removed.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered service/config state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id 1b0321bf... and healthy state (crond active, cron.allow correct, enforcement denial for 'precheck') captured immediately before reboot. 'sudo -n systemctl reboot' returned exit 0 before disconnect (connection reset confirms in-flight ack). Post-restart boot_id changed to 74214009... (cross-checked against fixed after_executor snapshot), crond active, cron.allow intact, cron.deny absent, enforcement re-verified with 'postcheck' denied and opsadmin allowed.

requirements.requirement: No leftover test artifacts or unintended users after completion
requirements.summary: Final state shows only 'opsadmin' as the non-system user, cron.allow=root/opsadmin, cron.deny absent, empty crontab spool dir, and no failed services or stray temp files in the after_executor lifecycle snapshot beyond expected boot-scoped systemd-private directories.

overall_summary: The task's material outcome — restricting cron scheduling to root and opsadmin via /etc/cron.allow with /etc/cron.deny removed — is directly demonstrated as configured and enforced, both before and after a full node restart with proper boot-identity cross-checks. Enforcement was validated with correctly-impersonated non-listed users (cronprobe2, precheck, postcheck) denied, and opsadmin/root allowed. One early verification step was methodologically flawed (testing via root's '-u' flag instead of user impersonation) and briefly created an unintended crontab file for a non-permitted user, but this was fully cleaned up and does not affect the final state. Final system state is clean: only opsadmin exists as a non-system user, no failed services, no residual artifacts beyond expected boot-scoped temp directories.
limitations: The flawed 'cronprobe is denied' check in cmd-a9ea3e06f422425c does not actually validate per-user cron.allow enforcement (root using 'crontab -u <user>' bypasses the restriction), so that specific piece of evidence should not be relied upon; the later cronprobe2 test correctly supersedes it.

Post-restart persistence of the cron.allow configuration was only verified once, immediately after the single reboot; no evidence of behavior across multiple reboot cycles or crond's actual execution of a scheduled job over time.

operational_hygiene.summary: All executor commands were either read-only discovery, directly implementing the cron.allow restriction, or verification/cleanup of temporary test users (cronprobe, cronprobe2, precheck, postcheck) — all fully removed by task end. One flawed verification step in cmd-a9ea3e06f422425c used 'sudo -n bash -c ... crontab -u cronprobe -' (root installing on behalf of cronprobe) rather than impersonating the user directly; this bypassed the restriction being tested, producing a misleading pass and creating a stray crontab spool file for a non-permitted user. It was bounded, low-risk, and fully reverted (user deleted and spool file explicitly removed in cmd-9d58871dfa024765), but it counts as an unnecessary/flawed mutation since it did not validly contribute to the verification outcome. Two commands had transient non-zero/failure artifacts (cmd-43999c3f12cc4de6 userdel failing due to a running process, and cmd-0048933f29d04817 referencing an already-deleted postcheck user) which were immediately and correctly resolved, not residue.
